How seasons affect our moods
四季如何影响我们的情绪
词汇：seasons 四季
1 We have four seasons in the UK. I like to think that spring gets its name from the
flowers springing up to bloom. Next is my personal favourite – summer. I love the
long, balmy evenings. Autumn, as some call fall, comes after. It's characterised by
the orange and red leaves. Winter rolls around, and most of the vegetation is
either decomposing or already dead, and the days are short and gloomy.
2 It's no wonder that, according to the Royal College of Psychiatrists, about three in
every hundred people in the UK experience seasonal affective disorder, otherwise
known as SAD. However, researchers at the Royal College of Psychiatrists have
discovered that all seasons have an impact on our psychological functioning. It's
also been found that hormones play an important role in seasonal mood changes
as they fluctuate throughout the year.
3 An article published on Springer Nature Link observes positive emotional and
physical changes to volunteers who were exposed to UVA from the Sun. Serotonin,
known as 'the happy hormone', and dopamine, which is linked to motivation and
pleasure, increases in months where there is a boost of sunlight. Similarly, lovers
of spring recalibrate their energy and mood. After the cold, dark seasons of
autumn and winter, it can feel like a biological reset.
4 Speaking of cold and dark, this is when those with naturally higher serotonin levels
feel their mood regulating. They no longer feel overwhelmed by the high-level
serotonin seasons of spring and summer. Reduced sunlight triggers higher
melatonin, the sleepy hormone. There is the notion of preparing to slow down and
get cosy, like that of animals in hibernation. It also rains more in autumn and
winter. The Mind Company says that rain sounds reduce cortisol, the stress
hormone, and helps you relax, focus and even sleep better.
5 We might like one season more than others. Our experience of seasons differs
depending on location and environment. But one thing is for sure – our feelings
change from season to season, and recognising these changes can help us act in
ways that are in-line with our mental, emotional and physical capabilities.

When we welcome a new season, our hormones fluctuate. This triggers some
changes in how we feel and behave. Some of us feel like we need a boost in sunlight

help regulate your emotions and direct your actions more positively.
